editor_spans.body: Burnham's speech in Motherwell explains Ravenscraig and the Leigh pits as decisions taken by distant people who never had to live with the results. That is only half the story. Those closures came from national choices about steel, coal and exposure to world markets. A more local decision-maker would not have kept them open.

Devolving decisions does not by itself reverse deindustrialisation. Money and markets have to follow. The concrete sums in the speech are small against a 30-year hole: £10 million, matched by Holyrood, for two defence colleges, and £1 billion of research funding spread across the whole UK. The danger is that 'power to places' hands regions responsibility for decline without the means to fix it.

The speech has a tension at its core. Burnham lists public control of water and public ownership of rail as devolution's proudest achievements. He then calls Scotland one of Europe's most centralised nations. Those achievements are themselves acts of central consolidation. The government he leads is doing the same with Great British Railways. The real dividing line is not centralisation against devolution. It is which centre gets the power.

The most concrete item is the offer to devolve DWP employment support to Scotland. That is a genuine concession on a reserved power. It also sets a political trap. Burnham says only party politics could stop cooperation, so a refusal by the SNP government can be framed as putting party before place. 'Problem-solving, not point-scoring' is itself a way of scoring.

The bus-procurement story is the clearest sign of his industrial thinking: pay more to buy British because the money circulates back into communities. Applied UK-wide, that means openly accepting higher public costs. It will also run into procurement and trade rules, at the same time as he seeks closer alignment with the EU. Reindustrialisation through public purchasing is a real policy, but not a free one.
